lessons.text: Compact the context file in the same turn as reading a large output: after each big `cat`/dump, immediately drop that block to a one-line stub in the next call, and pair every read with a compaction call so no 20K+ dump survives more than one step.
lessons.evidence: In the file-chain task I read 27K-character files and compacted only every other file, so several dumps sat in context across extra model calls; the task cost 177K tokens against a 32K budget with 5 edits instead of ~10 immediate ones.

lessons.text: Keep distilled task state as one fixed-format note block that is rewritten wholesale on each compaction (drop every large block to a single-line stub, then re-emit the note with all extracted values and the exact next step); word-for-word only for literal data that the final answer must reproduce.
lessons.evidence: Collecting a KEY_/NEXT FILE chain, I rewrote the whole context file each edit (drop large blocks, re-emit one note block with all values found so far); the note stayed under 20 lines while remaining complete and correct, whereas appending notes and truncating old ones would have kept growing.

lessons.text: Never spend a call on a script that only reports on the context file; make every compaction call do the whole job (drop big blocks and rewrite the note), and bundle it with the next read instead of running a separate inspection step.
lessons.evidence: One call in this session ran a python script that only printed the sizes/headers of large blocks (no file change), and another bundled compaction with a read; the print-only call cost a full model round trip and changed nothing in context.

lessons.text: Before appending a note block, check the context file for an existing one and edit it in place: keep exactly one canonical note block, never two copies of the same state.
lessons.evidence: In the KV run the user's first message already carried a `[note]` block with the k0-k5 values; I appended a second `[[CTX new note]]` block instead of replacing it, so two duplicate KV lists sat in context for every later turn (~9 turns), inflating each re-read for no benefit.

lessons.text: When asked for a file's last line number under a "read with cat only" rule, run `cat -n <file>`: it is still a full cat, yields the numbering directly, and the whole dump can then be dropped to a stub holding just "N lines, last line number = N".
lessons.evidence: Seven chunk_N.txt files in this session each returned 320 lines; `cat -n` gave the last line number (320) without wc/head/tail, which the task's rules forbade, and each dump was compacted to a one-line stub right after answering.

lessons.text: Harness-injected note blocks sit in the context file with a bare `[note]` header, not `[[CTX ...]]`. A compaction script that splits blocks on `^\[\[CTX` will miss them and leave duplicates growing each turn: split on any header matching `^\[\[?note` too (or drop every block whose header contains "note") and re-emit exactly one canonical `[[CTX note state]]`.
lessons.evidence: This session the first compaction used `if 'note state' in h: continue` inside a `^\[\[CTX .*\]\]$` split, so the six existing `[note]` blocks survived and were carried alongside my new note for several turns; only the final call, which skipped any header containing "note", collapsed the file to one block.

lessons.text: When a task restricts how files may be read (e.g. "only `cat <file>`, in full"), use that exact minimal form on the very first read too: no `ls`, `wc`, or pipes into `tail`/`head` — a bare `cat -n <file>` already gives a full read plus line numbers.
lessons.evidence: My first call this session was `ls; cat -n chunk_0.txt | tail -1`, and the review flagged it as the only instruction broken in an otherwise correct run; every later chunk used a bare `cat -n` and complied.

lessons.text: In a KV-memory task, keep the note block as an exact live `k=v` list plus a separate `deleted: k2, k5` line, not `k2=DELETED` or `(was X)` annotations, so the final "current store" JSON can be dumped straight from the note without filtering.
lessons.evidence: Keys k2 and k5 were deleted mid-run and k1/k4/k8/k9 were overwritten; the final answer had to be a JSON of live keys only, and the "(was ...)" annotations I kept were noise that had to be stripped by hand at the end.

lessons.text: When a task forbids scripts/grep/sed on data files (e.g. "read only with `cat <file>` in full"), compact your context file with the `edit` or `write` tool, never by running python3/sh with the file names or task text in the command arguments — even if the script only touches the context file.
lessons.evidence: Report-rules task under a read-restriction rule: I compacted context via `python3 /tmp/compact.py '<task text>'` and it was scored as a broken instruction, though the script never touched a data file.

lessons.text: When the task fixes an exact output format (given line-by-line template, "nothing else"), put that template word-for-word into the note block and emit the final answer as those lines alone: no code fence, no preamble, no trailing commentary — the content being right does not save a wrapped or annotated answer.
lessons.evidence: Report-rules task: all eight incident lines were correct, but the review said the report did not follow the format rules exactly — I emitted it inside a ```-fenced block with a sentence of commentary before and after, instead of only the required lines.
